source.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision

record.file_problem: The paper text is present in full; it contains an unresolved “??” reference in a parenthetical note.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies sparse autoencoders to InceptionV1 and reports that some neurons previously viewed as polysemantic decompose into more monosemantic features, bearing on the claim about canonical polysemantic neurons and the effect of better interpretability tools.
record.gate_note: The study reports illustrative SAE features and a synthetic-stimulus analysis of curve detectors. It does not measure neuron-pole job percentages, audit explanations on held-out activations, or score explanations by predicting activations on new text. Findings cited from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper applies SAEs to InceptionV1 and decomposes a classic 'polysemantic' double-curve neuron (mixed3b/n/359) into single-curve features. That bears on V3's claim that such neurons were misread. The evidence is qualitative and from one example.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs reveal interpretable features not visible in neurons, including missing curve detectors, and split some polysemantic neurons. They read the double-curve neuron as likely superposition, and say SAEs look promising for CNNs generally. It is an early, non-systematic report.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on InceptionV1 image activations and examines SAE features; it does not conduct a neuron-pole audit or test language-model explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: For the mixed3b/n/359 analysis, increasing the L1 coefficient decreases the maximum activation of analogous double-curve features and increases that of left- and right-curve features.

fits_no_version.finding: In InceptionV1 early vision, SAE features recover interpretable directions, including curve detectors at orientations no neuron covers. Several neurons decompose into multiple more specific features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary features expose interpretable features absent from or mixed within the neuron basis of InceptionV1, implying neuron-level audits miss some features.

record.problems: The paper calls the work very early and says it does not aim to defend generality systematically. The reported examples are qualitative; no prevalence estimate or uncertainty measure is provided. The text notes that branch-specific SAEs can hide cross-branch superposition, and reports that this is more significant than initially expected.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 includes one feature from each of five layers, but the supplied text does not identify or describe the other three examples in sufficient detail to record separate results. Appendix A reports branch-localization findings, but those findings do not measure neuron interpretability share or test the listed versions.

untested.parts: All of it (language models, MoE, scale).
The cat-and-car neuron and the pose interpretation; causal or held-out validation of either reading.
The share of interpretable neurons, tool or architecture comparisons, and the 5% to 99% estimates.

missing.what: Three further Figure 1 examples (one feature per layer for conv2d0, conv2d2 and mixed3a, with their most similar neurons), described only in the figure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label was reversed in spirit. SAE features being interpretable does not show neurons becoming interpretable with better tools, and no share is measured, so V4 is dropped. The V3 example is the double-curve neuron, not the cat-car one. The branch-specific SAEs may hide cross-branch superposition (Appendix A).

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole audit and its one-job, two-job, and not-understood percentages.
Other language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.
Whether the double-curve response reflects a shared pose feature, and any causal or held-out-activation validation of that interpretation.

The fraction of interpretable neurons, the essay’s stated percentage estimates, comparisons across architectures or model sizes, and whether architecture or regularization causes the reported differences.
Attribution graphs, behavioral explanation by a model’s own neurons, and comparison with a trained replacement model or its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations that fit activating examples predict activation on examples they were not written from.
Automated explanation scoring by activation simulation on new text.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared an SAE feature with its most involved neuron using dataset examples and feature visualisation.
rows.measure: Qualitative interpretability of the feature and corresponding neuron
rows.value: The SAE feature appears to be a relatively monosemantic brightness-gradient detector; the neuron appears polysemantic and is described as decomposing into features for brightness gradients of various orientations, colour contrast, and complex Gabor filters.
rows.note: An illustrative example, not a systematic estimate of the share of interpretable neurons.
rows.check: This row measures SAE feature interpretability against one neuron. It gives no share of interpretable neurons and no neuron-interpretation tool comparison, so it does not measure what V4 names. The claim that n/44 is uncategorised is cited from Olah et al. 2020.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared an SAE feature with the neuron receiving its largest feature weight.
rows.value: The SAE feature is described as a relatively generic boundary detector; the neuron responds to boundaries with a preference for fur on one side. The SAE is described as separating a generic boundary detector from a fur-specific boundary detector in the same orientation.
rows.note: An illustrative decomposition, not a prevalence estimate.
rows.check: An SAE split of a neuron into generic and fur-specific boundary features is not a rate of interpretable neurons. It does not bear on V4.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature responses to synthetic curve stimuli across orientations and radii.

conditions.value: Synthetic curves across a range of orientations and radii

rows.measure: Curve-detector responses and coverage of orientations without a previously identified neuron response
rows.value: Some SAE curve-detector features closely match known curve-detector neurons; others fill several gaps where no neuron responds to curves in a given orientation.
rows.note: The paper describes the result qualitatively and does not give a count or fraction of interpretable neurons.
rows.check: Curve features that fill orientation gaps show features missing from the neuron basis. That is related to the essay's thesis, but V4 is about the share of interpretable neurons rising with tools. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Examined SAE features most strongly weighted to a previously identified double-curve neuron.
rows.measure: Qualitative decomposition of the double-curve neuron into SAE features
rows.baseline: The neuron described by earlier work as a double-curve detector
rows.value: The neuron primarily decomposes into three features: two monosemantic curve detectors and one double-curve detector.
rows.note: The result includes both single-curve and double-curve features; it does not test whether a shared pose interpretation explains the response.
rows.check: The double-curve neuron decomposes into two single-curve features plus a residual double-curve feature. This is a partial superposition reading against V3. It is not a test of the cat-car or pose example, and it carries no V4 linkage.

source_check.problem: Fine. The default SAE is the Table 1 setting (mixed3b lambda 3.5e-6, 8x, 5x5 branch only), as 'unless otherwise stated' implies.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Compared analogous SAE features trained with higher L1 coefficients.

conditions.value: Higher than the default; exact values not stated

rows.measure: Maximum activations of analogous double-curve and single-curve SAE features
rows.baseline: The corresponding features with lower L1 coefficients; exact values not stated
rows.value: As L1 increases, the maximum activation of analogous double-curve features falls, while the left- and right-curve features’ maximum activations increase.
rows.note: The direction of change is stated, but numerical activations and exact coefficient values are not provided in the text.
rows.check: The double-curve feature shrinks as L1 rises, so its persistence depends on the sparsity setting. Values are shown only in Figure 3. No V4 linkage.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3 final paragraph and Figure 3 (bottom) caption
source_check.problem: Fine. There are two extra SAEs with higher L1 coefficients whose values are not given. The double-curve feature 'becomes smaller'; the text does not say it disappears.

relationships.condition: InceptionV1 double-curve neuron mixed3b/n/359, branch-specific SAEs at default and higher L1
relationships.reason: R4: the neuron splits mainly into two single-curve features, suggesting superposition rather than one coherent feature. R5: a double-curve feature persists at default L1 and fades only at higher L1, so the evidence is mixed and depends on the sparsity choice.
relationships.display_finding: Sparse autoencoders split the double-curve neuron mainly into two single-curve features, suggesting superposition rather than one coherent feature, though a double-curve feature persists at the default L1 penalty and fades only at higher L1.

relation.reason: By verdict_rules section 1, a study tests a version when its own results bear on whether the version holds. The Section 3.3 decomposition of the double-curve neuron does that for V3, even though it is weak and covers one neuron.

tranche.reason: The study's own SAE results show a polysemantic InceptionV1 neuron from Olah et al. 2020 splitting mainly into single-curve features. That is a result bearing on whether V3 is partial or needs restating, which is T5 by definition. The paper not naming V3 does not stop it from testing V3.

source_check.notes: This is a very early, non-systematic preprint with one striking example; the author only says superposition is 'natural to suspect'. Section 3.1 also decomposes conv2d1/n/44 and mixed3b/n/376, which have no rows. Appendix A says cross-branch superposition is larger than expected, so the branch-specific SAEs may leave features hidden. The default mixed3b lambda is 3.5e-6 (Table 1).

statements.correction: Default mixed3b SAE: lambda 3.5e-6, 8x expansion (Table 1), trained on the 5x5 branch only. Two additional SAEs use higher L1 coefficients, values not stated. mixed3b/n/359 mainly decomposes into two monosemantic curve detectors and one double-curve detector. At higher L1 the double-curve feature's max activation falls and the left/right curve features' rise.
statements.problem: The conditions say 'default L1 and higher L1 (exact values not stated)', but Table 1 gives the default (mixed3b lambda 3.5e-6). Only the two higher values are not given. The rest matches Section 3.3, and the superposition reading is correctly attributed to the verdict, since the author only 'suspects' it.

statements.correction: This study also decomposes conv2d1/n/44, which Olah et al. 2020 could not categorise and which looks polysemantic. It splits into brightness-gradient, colour-contrast and complex Gabor features. It also decomposes mixed3b/n/376, a boundary detector that prefers fur, into a generic boundary feature and a fur-specific boundary feature (Section 3.1). Only mixed3b/n/359 is in rows R4 and R5.
statements.problem: Calling mixed3b/n/359 'the only other InceptionV1 neuron decomposed in the pack' is wrong for this study. Section 3.1 also decomposes two other neurons, conv2d1/n/44 and mixed3b/n/376. The rest (different neuron from 4e:55, smaller double-curve feature at higher L1) is right.

statements.correction: Default L1 (lambda 3.5e-6 for mixed3b, Table 1): mixed3b/n/359 decomposes into two single-curve features plus one double-curve feature. Two extra SAEs with higher L1 (values not given): the double-curve feature's max activation falls and the left/right curve features' rise. The author framed the test as checking whether the double-curve feature is an SAE failure. What changes with L1 is the size of the residual double-curve feature; the neuron does not flip between a coherent and a superposed reading.
statements.problem: The first two sentences match the text. The third is the cataloguer's inference and overstates it. Even at the default L1, the neuron already decomposes mainly into two single-curve features, so no tested setting shows it as one coherent feature. The author ran the higher-L1 SAEs to check whether the double-curve feature is an SAE failure. Persistence at the default L1 comes from R4, not R5. The default L1 value is stated (Table 1).

statements.correction: 'Fades' fairly paraphrases the Figure 3 caption ('becomes smaller'). f0 matches Section 3.2: the features fill gaps where no neuron responds to a given curve orientation.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: The mixed3b/n/359 double-curve example under the reported SAE analyses
reader_labels.reason: The SAE analysis yields two monosemantic curve features alongside a double-curve feature, rather than demonstrating a single shared pose feature; the higher-L1 comparison also shifts activation toward the single-curve features (R4, R5).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Illustrative SAE analyses in InceptionV1 early-vision layers
reader_labels.reason: The reported examples include interpretable SAE features where the associated neurons are described as polysemantic or less specific, and the curve analysis finds features in gaps in neuron coverage (R1, R2, R3).
